mcqs.question: A pipeline closes each one-minute window the instant its processing-time clock crosses the minute boundary. What goes wrong with out-of-order data?
options: Nothing — processing time and event time always advance together
An event whose event time belongs to that minute but arrives late gets excluded, because the window already closed before it showed up
The window simply takes longer to close, but the result stays correct
The pipeline crashes when it detects an out-of-order event
mcqs.explanation: Closing on processing time alone assumes every event for that minute has already arrived, which out-of-order delivery violates — a late event's window has already fired without it. It doesn't crash or self-correct; the result is simply short a data point.

mcqs.question: What does a watermark of value W formally claim?
options: That every event with event time before W has definitely already been processed
That no event with event time earlier than W will ever arrive, with absolute certainty
That the system does not expect any more events with event time earlier than W, though it could still be wrong
That the current wall-clock time is W
mcqs.explanation: A watermark is a heuristic estimate of completeness, not a guarantee — late data arriving behind an already-passed watermark is exactly the failure mode the rest of the topic addresses. It's unrelated to wall-clock time and doesn't promise processing has finished, only that no earlier event is expected.

mcqs.question: A team tightens their watermark's slack to get faster dashboard updates. What's the direct cost of that choice?
options: Higher end-to-end latency for every window
The watermark will stop advancing entirely
Windowing logic must be rewritten to use processing time instead
More events will be classified as late and dropped or side-outputted
mcqs.explanation: A tighter watermark fires windows sooner, which is exactly what lowers latency — but it also means more genuinely-out-of-order events arrive after their window has already closed, increasing late/dropped data. It doesn't stop the watermark from advancing, and it doesn't require switching away from event time.

mcqs.question: A window has already fired its result, but an event for that window arrives within the configured allowed-lateness period. What happens?
options: The window's state is still open, so the event can update the result before it's finalized for good
The event is silently discarded because the window already fired
The event is automatically routed to a side output regardless of timing
The pipeline restarts the window from scratch
mcqs.explanation: Allowed lateness keeps a window's state open past the watermark specifically so events arriving within that grace period can still revise the result. Side outputs are for data arriving after even that grace period elapses, and nothing here restarts or discards the window.

mcqs.question: In a job reading from 100 partitions, one partition falls badly behind due to a downstream bottleneck. What happens to the job's watermark, assuming the standard minimum-across-partitions computation?
options: The watermark ignores the stalled partition and advances based on the other 99
The watermark advances at the average rate across all 100 partitions
The watermark is held back to match the stalled partition, delaying every window across every key
Only windows for keys on the stalled partition are delayed; others are unaffected
mcqs.explanation: Because the watermark is typically the minimum across all inputs, one stalled partition holds back the entire combined watermark, delaying every window regardless of which key it belongs to. It isn't excluded or averaged away automatically — that requires deliberate handling like idleness detection.

mcqs.question: A partition has no traffic at all for an hour because its key range is simply inactive. Why can this stall the pipeline's watermark even though nothing is actually broken?
options: Idle partitions are automatically dropped from the topic
The minimum-across-partitions watermark can't advance past an idle partition's last known timestamp unless it's explicitly excluded
This only happens if the partition also has a network failure
Idle partitions cause the aggregation logic to throw an error
mcqs.explanation: With no new events, an idle partition never advances its own timestamp, and since the combined watermark takes the minimum across partitions, it stalls at that partition's last value unless an idleness timeout excludes it. Nothing is dropped or erroring — the data is simply absent.
